## Overview

This is the dataset from my own Discussion 5A post. A population report
counts how many copies of each trading card have been graded at each
grade. The questions from my post: **what share of each card's graded
copies earned a 10 (its gem rate), does 1st Edition grade better than
later printings, and which cards are hardest to get a 10 on?**

## Data source

The data comes from PriceCharting's population report for the Pokémon
Base Set (<https://www.pricecharting.com/pop/set/pokemon-base-set>).
Grading companies like PSA and CGC score cards on a 1 to 10 scale, and a
population report counts how many copies of each card have received each
grade. PriceCharting combines PSA and CGC counts into one number and
folds half grades (for example 8.5) into the nearest whole grade below.

I copied the table into `pokemon_base_set_pop_wide.csv` exactly as it
appears on the page, sorted by popularity, on October 8, 2026. Nothing
was cleaned by hand: counts keep their thousands commas, missing values
keep their "-" character, and sealed products (booster boxes and packs)
stay in the file. The CSV holds the first 141 rows of the report as the
page loaded them, which are the most popular items, not all 466 items
the site lists for the set.

```{r setup}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(knitr)

# One shared look for every chart in this project
theme_p2 <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      legend.position  = "top"
    )
}

# The holo vs. non-holo chart jitters its points, so fix the random seed
set.seed(607)

variant_colors <- c(
  "1st Edition" = "#2c5f8a",
  "Shadowless"  = "#c9701a",
  "Unlimited"   = "#8a9bab"
)
```

## Data structure before tidying

Every column is read as text on purpose, so R does not guess types or
turn the "-" characters into anything before I decide how to handle
them.

```{r import}
csv_url <- paste0(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dillonleeper/",
  "DATA-607/main/assignments/week06/project2/pokemon/pokemon_base_set_pop_wide.csv"
)

# Try the GitHub copy first; fall back to the local copy if it can't be reached
read_raw <- function(path) {
  read_csv(
    path,
    col_types = cols(.default = col_character()),
    na        = character()   # keep "-" and blanks exactly as they are
  )
}
raw_pop <- tryCatch(read_raw(csv_url), error = function(e) read_raw("pokemon_base_set_pop_wide.csv"))

glimpse(raw_pop)
```

The raw file has **`r nrow(raw_pop)` rows** and **`r ncol(raw_pop)`
columns**: `r paste(names(raw_pop), collapse = ", ")`.

```{r raw-sample}
raw_pop |>
  slice(c(1, 2, 8, 12)) |>
  kable(caption = "Representative raw rows (wide format)")
```

What makes this untidy:

- **Grade lives in the headers.** "Grade 6" through "Grade 10" are
  values of one variable, so each row holds five separate observations.
- **One column holds three variables.** "Charizard \[1st Edition\] #4"
  packs the card name, the printing, and the card number into one
  string.
- **Total does not match the visible columns.** For unlimited Charizard,
  grades 6 to 10 add up to 59,711 but Total says 99,255, because grades
  1 to 5 are counted in Total without having their own columns.
- **Numbers are stored as text.** Commas ("17,851") and the "-"
  placeholder make every count column character data.
- **Some rows are not cards at all.** Booster boxes and packs have "-"
  in every column.

## Transformation steps

### Step 1: Rename columns to snake_case

```{r rename}
pop_named <- raw_pop |>
  rename_with(~ .x |> str_to_lower() |> str_replace_all("\\s+", "_"))

names(pop_named)
```

### Step 2: Handle missing values and convert counts to numbers

Decision: a "-" in a count column means the report has no copies
recorded at that grade. I first turn it into `NA`, then `parse_number()`
strips the commas.

```{r clean-values}
dash_pattern <- "^[-\\u2212\\u2013]$"   # hyphen, minus sign, or en dash

pop_numeric <- pop_named |>
  mutate(across(
    grade_6:total,
    ~ parse_number(if_else(
      str_detect(str_trim(.x), dash_pattern), NA_character_, str_trim(.x)
    ))
  ))

pop_numeric |> filter(is.na(total)) |> select(card, total)
```

Decision: rows with a missing **Total** are sealed products or variants
that have never been graded. They have no grade data to analyze, so I
drop them. For the remaining cards, a missing grade count means zero
graded copies at that grade, so it becomes 0.

```{r drop-sealed}
dropped_rows <- pop_numeric |> filter(is.na(total))

pop_cards <- pop_numeric |>
  filter(!is.na(total)) |>
  mutate(across(grade_6:grade_10, ~ replace_na(.x, 0)))
```

This removes **`r nrow(dropped_rows)` rows**
(`r paste(dropped_rows$card, collapse = "; ")`), leaving
**`r nrow(pop_cards)` graded cards**.

### Step 3: Split the card column into name, variant, and number

`extract()` uses a regular expression with three groups: the name, an
optional bracketed variant, and the card number after "\#". A card with
no bracket is the regular Unlimited printing.

```{r split-card}
pop_split <- pop_cards |>
  extract(
    card,
    into   = c("card_name", "variant", "card_number"),
    regex  = "^(.*?)\\s*(?:\\[(.*)\\])?\\s*#(\\d+)$",
    remove = FALSE
  ) |>
  mutate(
    variant     = coalesce(na_if(variant, ""), "Unlimited"),
    card_number = as.integer(card_number),
    rarity      = if_else(card_number <= 16, "Holo rare", "Non-holo")
  )

# Every card must parse cleanly
stopifnot(!any(is.na(pop_split$card_name)), !any(is.na(pop_split$card_number)))

pop_split |> count(variant, sort = TRUE) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Variant", "Cards"), caption = "Printings after the split")
```

Cards numbered 1 to 16 are the Base Set holo rares, so I add a `rarity`
column from the card number.

### Step 4: Recover the hidden grades 1 to 5

Total includes grades 1 to 5, which have no columns. Instead of ignoring
the mismatch, I compute the missing count so every graded copy is
accounted for.

```{r recover-low}
pop_full <- pop_split |>
  mutate(grade_1_to_5 = total - (grade_6 + grade_7 + grade_8 + grade_9 + grade_10))

# A negative count would mean the source columns are inconsistent
stopifnot(all(pop_full$grade_1_to_5 >= 0))

pop_full |>
  filter(card == "Charizard #4") |>
  select(card, grade_6:grade_10, grade_1_to_5, total) |>
  kable(format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
        caption = "Unlimited Charizard: grades 1 to 5 explain the gap")
```

### Step 5: Pivot from wide to long

Each row becomes one card at one grade. Total is now redundant (it
equals the sum of `population` for each card), so I check that and then
leave it out.

```{r pivot}
grade_levels <- c("1-5", "6", "7", "8", "9", "10")

pop_tidy <- pop_full |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols         = c(grade_1_to_5, grade_6:grade_10),
    names_to     = "grade",
    names_prefix = "grade_",
    values_to    = "population"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    grade = str_replace(grade, "_to_", "-"),
    grade = factor(grade, levels = grade_levels)
  ) |>
  select(card, card_name, variant, card_number, rarity, grade, population)

# The long data must add back up to the original totals
check <- pop_tidy |>
  group_by(card) |>
  summarise(population = sum(population)) |>
  left_join(select(pop_full, card, total), by = "card")
stopifnot(all(check$population == check$total))

head(pop_tidy, 12) |> kable(caption = "Tidy data: one row per card per grade")
```

The tidy table has **`r nrow(pop_tidy)` rows** (`r nrow(pop_full)` cards
× 6 grade groups) and 7 columns.

## Analytical methods

All analysis below uses only `pop_tidy`.

- **Gem rate** = grade 10 copies ÷ all graded copies of that card. It is
  the share of submissions that came back a perfect 10.
- **Hardest 10s** ranks cards by lowest gem rate. I only rank cards with
  at least 500 graded copies so a card with 3 graded copies cannot top
  the list.
- **Printing comparison** uses the cards that appear in all three main
  printings (1st Edition, Shadowless, Unlimited). I report both the
  pooled gem rate (all copies together) and the median card's gem rate,
  because one huge card (unlimited Charizard) can dominate a pooled
  number.
- **Holo vs. non-holo** compares pooled gem rates by rarity. Cards #1 to
  16 are the holo rares.
- The only randomness is the jitter in the holo chart, so
  `set.seed(607)` in the setup chunk keeps it the same on every render.

```{r gem-rate}
gem <- pop_tidy |>
  group_by(card, card_name, variant, card_number, rarity) |>
  summarise(
    graded   = sum(population),
    grade_10 = sum(population[grade == "10"]),
    .groups  = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(gem_rate = grade_10 / graded)

overall_rate <- sum(gem$grade_10) / sum(gem$graded)
```

Across all `r nrow(gem)` cards there are **`r comma(sum(gem$graded))`
graded copies**, and **`r percent(overall_rate, accuracy = 0.1)`** of
them are 10s.

## Analysis 1: Which cards are hardest to get a 10 on?

```{r hardest-table}
hardest <- gem |>
  filter(graded >= 500) |>
  arrange(gem_rate) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

hardest |>
  transmute(
    Card              = card,
    Rarity            = rarity,
    `Graded copies`   = comma(graded),
    `Grade 10 copies` = comma(grade_10),
    `Gem rate (%)`    = percent(gem_rate, accuracy = 0.01)
  ) |>
  kable(caption = "10 lowest gem rates (cards with 500+ graded copies)")
```

```{r hardest-chart}
#| fig-height: 5
hardest |>
  mutate(card = reorder(card, -gem_rate)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gem_rate, y = card, fill = variant)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = variant_colors, drop = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "The hardest Base Set cards to grade a 10",
    x     = "Gem rate (share of graded copies that earned a 10)",
    y     = NULL,
    fill  = "Printing"
  ) +
  theme_p2()
```

Every card on this list is a holo rare. Unlimited Charizard has the
lowest gem rate at
**`r percent(hardest$gem_rate[1], accuracy = 0.01)`**: only
`r comma(hardest$grade_10[1])` 10s out of `r comma(hardest$graded[1])`
graded copies. Eight of the ten are Shadowless printings, a short early
print run of the set. Holo foil scratches easily and the holo window
shows every flaw, which fits what collectors say about these cards.

## Analysis 2: Does 1st Edition grade better than Shadowless or Unlimited?

```{r printing-compare}
main_printings <- c("1st Edition", "Shadowless", "Unlimited")

# Cards that exist in all three main printings
in_all_three <- gem |>
  filter(variant %in% main_printings) |>
  count(card_name) |>
  filter(n == 3) |>
  pull(card_name)

printing_summary <- gem |>
  filter(variant %in% main_printings, card_name %in% in_all_three) |>
  group_by(variant) |>
  summarise(
    cards           = n(),
    graded          = sum(graded),
    grade_10        = sum(grade_10),
    median_gem_rate = median(gem_rate),
    .groups         = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(pooled_gem_rate = grade_10 / graded) |>
  arrange(desc(pooled_gem_rate))

printing_summary |>
  transmute(
    Printing                  = variant,
    Cards                     = cards,
    `Graded copies`           = comma(graded),
    `Grade 10 copies`         = comma(grade_10),
    `Pooled gem rate (%)`     = percent(pooled_gem_rate, accuracy = 0.1),
    `Median card gem rate (%)`= percent(median_gem_rate, accuracy = 0.1)
  ) |>
  kable(caption = "Gem rate by printing (cards found in all three printings)")
```

```{r printing-chart}
#| fig-height: 5
pop_tidy |>
  filter(variant %in% main_printings, card_name %in% in_all_three) |>
  group_by(variant, grade) |>
  summarise(population = sum(population), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(variant) |>
  mutate(share = population / sum(population)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = grade, y = share, fill = variant)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = variant_colors) +
  labs(
    title = "Grade distribution by printing",
    subtitle = paste(length(in_all_three), "cards found in all three printings"),
    x     = "Grade",
    y     = "Share of graded copies",
    fill  = "Printing"
  ) +
  theme_p2()
```

```{r printing-p}
first_ed <- filter(printing_summary, variant == "1st Edition")
shadow   <- filter(printing_summary, variant == "Shadowless")
unlim    <- filter(printing_summary, variant == "Unlimited")
```

For the `r length(in_all_three)` cards that exist in all three
printings, 1st Edition has the highest pooled gem rate at
**`r percent(first_ed$pooled_gem_rate, accuracy = 0.1)`**, compared with
`r percent(shadow$pooled_gem_rate, accuracy = 0.1)` for Shadowless and
`r percent(unlim$pooled_gem_rate, accuracy = 0.1)` for Unlimited. The
median card tells the same story for 1st Edition
(`r percent(first_ed$median_gem_rate, accuracy = 0.1)`), but Shadowless
has the lowest median
(`r percent(shadow$median_gem_rate, accuracy = 0.1)`). Unlimited's
pooled rate is pulled down mostly by unlimited Charizard, which alone
has `r comma(filter(gem, card == "Charizard #4")$graded)` graded copies.

One reason 1st Edition may grade better: owners of the most valuable
printing tend to submit only their best-looking copies, so the
submissions themselves are pre-screened. The data cannot separate print
quality from that selection.

## Analysis 3: Holo rares vs. non-holo cards

```{r rarity}
rarity_summary <- gem |>
  group_by(rarity) |>
  summarise(
    cards    = n(),
    graded   = sum(graded),
    grade_10 = sum(grade_10),
    .groups  = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(gem_rate = grade_10 / graded)

rarity_summary |>
  transmute(
    Rarity            = rarity,
    Cards             = cards,
    `Graded copies`   = comma(graded),
    `Grade 10 copies` = comma(grade_10),
    `Gem rate (%)`    = percent(gem_rate, accuracy = 0.1)
  ) |>
  kable(caption = "Gem rate by rarity")
```

```{r rarity-chart}
#| fig-height: 4
gem |>
  filter(graded >= 500) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rarity, y = gem_rate, color = rarity)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Holo rare" = "#2c5f8a", "Non-holo" = "#8a9bab")) +
  labs(
    title = "Holo rares rarely come back a 10",
    x     = NULL,
    y     = "Gem rate per card",
    color = "Rarity"
  ) +
  theme_p2()
```

```{r rarity-values}
holo     <- filter(rarity_summary, rarity == "Holo rare")
non_holo <- filter(rarity_summary, rarity == "Non-holo")
```

Holo rares gem at **`r percent(holo$gem_rate, accuracy = 0.1)`**, while
non-holo cards gem at
**`r percent(non_holo$gem_rate, accuracy = 0.1)`**, about
`r round(non_holo$gem_rate / holo$gem_rate)` times higher. This is the
largest difference in the project and explains why the hardest-10 list
is all holos.

## Conclusions

- Only `r percent(overall_rate, accuracy = 0.1)` of the
  `r comma(sum(gem$graded))` graded Base Set copies in this file are
  10s.
- Rarity matters more than printing: holo rares gem at
  `r percent(holo$gem_rate, accuracy = 0.1)` versus
  `r percent(non_holo$gem_rate, accuracy = 0.1)` for non-holos.
- Unlimited Charizard is the hardest 10 in the set at
  `r percent(hardest$gem_rate[1], accuracy = 0.01)`, which helps explain
  why a PSA 10 commands such a premium.
- 1st Edition copies earn 10s more often than Shadowless or Unlimited
  copies of the same cards
  (`r percent(first_ed$pooled_gem_rate, accuracy = 0.1)` pooled), though
  submission bias likely plays a role.

**Limitations.** PSA and CGC counts are combined, so the two companies'
standards cannot be compared. Half grades are folded into whole grades.
Some Unlimited holo counts look very low next to their Shadowless
counterparts (for example Venusaur), which suggests the source may file
many graded copies under a different printing label. The CSV covers the
first 141 rows of the report rather than all 466 items. Sale prices were
not part of this table, so the question of how scarcity at grade 10
drives price is left for future work.
